query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, the highly coherent interfaces between the alternating HEA layers serve as strong barriers to both dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby retarding time-dependent plastic deformation (creep).
generation.material_initial_state: A multilayer coating composed of high-entropy-alloy layers with a random polycrystalline structure and well-defined, coherent γ/γ′ interfaces established during deposition.
generation.intervention: Subject the multilayer coating to sustained elevated temperature and mechanical loading (creep conditions) and compare its performance to that of a monolithic HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–600 °C) and moderate applied stresses (e.g., 140–400 MPa), where both dislocation-mediated plasticity and diffusion processes contribute to creep.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent interfaces (γ/γ′ boundaries) between the layers.
generation.mechanism: These interfaces impede dislocation nucleation and glide by forcing dislocations to pile up rather than transmit freely between layers, and they also limit atomic diffusion along grain boundaries. This dual role reduces the rate at which plastic deformation progresses under sustained load, compared to structures lacking such interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical test conditions, the multilayer coating will exhibit a lower creep strain over time relative to a monolithic HEA coating. Microstructural analysis should reveal dislocation accumulation at interfaces and reduced signs of grain-boundary sliding in the multilayer configuration.
generation.baseline: Monolithic high-entropy-alloy coatings with similar overall composition and grain size but without a designed multilayer architecture.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under creep conditions where diffusion and dislocation activities dominate (e.g., intermediate temperature and moderate stress). Its applicability may be limited under very low temperatures or extremely high stresses where other mechanisms (such as phase transformations or dynamic recrystallization) might prevail.
generation.uncertainty: Although evidence supports interface-controlled creep resistance in γ/γ′-strengthened systems, the precise quantitative contribution of the coherent interfaces versus other microstructural factors (such as local chemical ordering) is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one set with a multilayer HEA structure featuring well-controlled, coherent interfaces, and another set as monolithic HEAs with an otherwise identical composition and similar grain size. Perform creep tests at 500–600 °C under controlled stress (e.g., 140–400 MPa). In addition, conduct in situ high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe dislocation behaviors and interface responses during loading.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves to compare deformation rates
Dislocation density and distribution analysis near interfaces via TEM
Interface coherence assessments before and after creep
Quantification of grain-boundary sliding or rotation using diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit significantly lower creep strain, or if the interfaces do not effectively block dislocation transfer (i.e., no pronounced dislocation pile-up at interfaces is observed) compared to the monolithic samples under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. In addition, increasing the γ′ volume fraction significantly enhances creep

Recently, Ding et al. synthesized FCC CoCrFeNiPd and CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. The former exhibited a higher yield strength than the latter with comparable tensile ductility. They proposed that the essential difference between these two HEAs was associated with atomic segregation and short-range ordering (SRO); both were enhanced in CoCrFeNiPd, as compared with CoCrFeNiMn. The idea was that SRO tends to create resistance to deformation/slip, leading to larger dislocation glide resistance in the more ordered CoCrFeNiPd than in CoCrFeNiMn HEAs. Theoretical work by Yin et al. suggested that the strengthening was due mainly to the large atomic/misfit volume of Pd in CoCrFeNi. Ma et al. identified a number of unusual features associated with dislocations/slips in HEAs that were related to lattice distortion and/or local chemical order. SRO also occurs in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). The atomic structure of a CoCrNi MEA indicates that Cr favors Ni and Co neighbors, reducing the electrical and thermal conductivities and increasing the stacking-fault energies and hardness.
